claims.text: High configurational entropy drives selective surface segregation of oxidation-active elements during early oxygen exposure.
Early oxidation of HEAs can cause element redistribution and composition changes at the surface.
Cr and Al are selectively segregated to the surface in the proposed HEAs.
Selective oxidation behavior in multielement alloys is governed in part by elemental redox tendencies and thermodynamics.
High configurational entropy retards bulk diffusion in the HEA.
High configurational entropy simultaneously facilitates selective surface segregation despite retarding bulk diffusion.
Oxidation-active elements rapidly form a thin, adherent, continuous protective oxide scale.
A CrTaO4-based external oxide scale can protect a refractory HEA during prolonged oxidation.
Al2O3 can occur within the external oxide scale of an oxidation-resistant refractory HEA.
The protective oxide scale acts as a barrier to further oxygen ingress and thereby lowers subsequent oxidation.
HEAs containing higher concentrations of Cr or Al will form thinner oxide scales than otherwise comparable controls.
HEAs containing higher concentrations of oxidation-active elements will form more continuous and less porous oxide scales.
HEAs containing higher concentrations of oxidation-active elements will exhibit lower oxidation mass gain.
Controls with reduced or less-segregating concentrations of oxidation-active elements will form thicker, less-adherent, and more-porous scales with higher mass gain.
A protective CrTaO4-based scale can remain relevant after oxidation at 1100°C for 200 hours.
The proposed entropy-driven segregation mechanism applies generally from approximately 900°C to 1100°C for exposures up to 200 hours.
Processing history, microstructural scale, and oxidation atmosphere may alter the proposed behavior.
Comparing Cr/Al-enriched and reduced-Cr/Al HEAs under identical oxidation conditions would test the proposed mechanism.
Failure of the enriched specimens to show both selective segregation and improved scale or mass-gain behavior would falsify selective segregation as the primary protective mechanism.
